items.title: Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’
items.summary:
The imprisonment of Russell Brand and allegations against David Walliams have prompted scrutiny of a culture that encouraged male transgression

In a 2008 episode of BBC Two’s comedy panel show Never Mind the Buzzcocks, the choreographer Arlene Phillips – the only woman on the programme – was told by the host Simon Amstell: “You look like you run a good whore house.” In reply, Phillips told a story with what appeared to be faux sincerity: while working with big stars, she explained, she would sometimes be asked to find dancers with “very special abilities” who might want to party after filming. Another panellist, the TV presenter Dermot O’Leary, mimed picking up a phone and said: “When you’re dancing tonight, do you mind having sex afterwards?” Everyone laughed.

Russell Brand’s imprisonment for rape and sexual assault this week, and allegations of sexual misconduct against the comedian and children’s author David Walliams have prompted scrutiny not only of the men involved, but of those who appeared to enable them. The chatshow host Jonathan Ross has apologised for a 2004 joke, in which he described the 15-year-old British comedy awards as being “like most 15-year-olds: drunk, unpredictable and probably going home with David Walliams”. The latter has denied the allegations made against him in reporting by the Guardian and ITV…
items.t: Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’

items.title: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood
items.summary:
After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook it for a joke that we were in on. In the age of lads’ mags, sex felt cheapened, yet somehow we were the ones who ended up paying for this. So it was doubly strange to sit in court and feel somehow complicit in it - in how this media culture had encouraged Russell Brand.

Continue reading...
items.t: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood

items.title: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
items.summary:
One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

Continue reading...
items.t: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?

items.title: Phil Collins Considers Touring Again After Years of Health Problems
items.summary:
Phil Collins has not given up on the possibility of touring again despite spending the better part of 20 years battling numerous health problems .

“Never say never … I do think, every now and again, that I’m not finished [touring],” Collins, 75, revealed in a recent interview with the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame . “On the other hand, I think of the practicalities.”

Those everyday “practicalities” would include giving up his current lifestyle for the grueling physical toll of life on the road.

“I’ll enjoy the sunshine, you know, just there’s no sweat, don’t have to do anything. Just get up and say, ‘What am I going to do today?'” he said. “But on the other hand, once you’ve been on stage all your life and tasted that, it’s difficult to stop.”

Phil Collins Hospitalized for Surgery: Report 

As for the possibility of releasing new music, Collins teased, “I’ve got ideas. I got things I finished. I’ve got things that I’ve half finished.”

Collins has struggled with various health issues, including type 2 diabetes, for many years. In February 2025, he told Mojo that he was no longer “hungry” to keep playing music because he’d been “very sick.”

The rocker suffered a serious spinal injury in 2007 that caused nerve damage. While the injury initially left him completely incapable of playing drums, he underwent corrective surgery in 2015.

Collins recovered well enough to reunite with Genesis bandmates Tony Banks and Mike Rutherford for the group’s The Last Domino? Tour in 2021, though his physical limitations mandated that Collins perform from a chair.

items.t: Phil Collins Considers Touring Again After Years of Health Problems

items.title: How Did Investigators Find Baby Who Survived Being Buried Alive? What to Know
items.summary:
The astonishing rescue of an 11-month-old baby who spent roughly 24 hours underground inside a dog crate has gripped a community in South Carolina and drawn national attention to a case authorities are calling miraculous.  

Koah Sharp was pulled from the dirt alive on November 10, 2026, after his father allegedly took him from a relative’s care and buried him in the woods near Batesburg-Leesville. 

Us breaks down what is known about how investigators located the boy, the charges against his father and the small details that may have saved Koah’s life. 

How Investigators Found Koah Sharp 
 A search party combing the area around the home of the suspect’s father noticed a patch of “freshly disturbed” dirt on the afternoon of November 10, 2026, according to Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon . 

Investigators began digging and soon heard the baby crying from beneath the soil, a sound Koon described at a news conference as “the most joyful sound.”  

Koah was found inside what Koon called a dog crate wrapped in a towel, and authorities believe that towel, combined with colder temperatures, likely created an air pocket that allowed him to survive. 

“So as you imagine, the race was on. Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out,” Koon said.  

The sheriff said Koah was “screaming at the top of his lungs” when rescuers reached him.  

He was rushed to a hospital and released that same evening, according to the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, which announced in a November 11 news release that “Koah Sharp is alive and well.”

items.title: Search Continues for Confidential Informant Who Vanished Over 10 Years Ago
items.summary:
A Pennsylvania woman’s disappearance remains unsolved more than 10 years after she vanished before she was set to testify as a confidential informant.

Investigators continue to search for Danielle M. Drozdowski , a Wilkes-Barre resident who went missing in 2014 at the age of 25, according to a Tuesday, November 10, news release from Pennsylvania State Police’s organization, PSP Tips.

Drozdowski “was a confidential informant who was scheduled to testify before a grand jury in August of 2014, however she failed to appear and was subsequently entered as ‘wanted,’” state police said.

Authorities are offering a $5,000 reward for information solving her disappearance. She would be 37 years old today.

Search Intensifies for Maine Teen Stefanie Damron 2 Years After She Vanished 

Family and friends haven’t seen or heard from Drozdowski since March 19, 2014, the last time she shared a post to Facebook, according to police.

“Her last known location and what she was last wearing are unknown,” police said.

Drozdowski is white, has blue eyes and is described as around 5-foot-2 or 5-foot-3, and weighing around 120 to 165 pounds by the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NamUs).

She also has several tattoos, including on both of her hands, her left arm and the back of her neck.

She has the outline of an “Om” symbol tattooed on her neck, according to NamUS. On her right hand, she has a tattoo of a possible shamrock. On her left arm, she has a multi-color skull tattoo and flowers.

She also has a tattoo of an anchor on her left hand.

“A rape conviction automatically carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison, but District Attorney Tony Clayton went a step further and filed the motion for castration,” the office said in a Friday, November 13, news release.

In 2024, Louisiana became the first state to legalize surgical castration as punishment for people convicted of sex crimes against a child younger than 12, according to the Associated Press . items.title: One leg in the air like you just don’t care? Eight classic power poses – and what they really mean
items.summary:
The pose of the moment is eye-catching and a little alarming. But it’s not the first to cause a stir. Here is a history of such stances, from the Angelina Jolie leg flash to Andrew Scott’s insouciant hand-in-pocket

You think you know your culture back to front, all the snooker moves that drove us to this point, and then something happens and you realise you haven’t been paying attention. I’m thinking of the modern celebrity power pose: one leg shooting high in the air, preferably while wearing a ballgown. It has to be a woman. If a man did it, he would be mocking a woman, making his power message: “I’m brave enough, and comfortable enough in my own skin, to mock ladies.” Which is powerful, to be fair.

When women do it – Victoria Beckham started it, Myleene Klass has dabbled, Amanda Holden does it all the time (even standing up) – other women liken them to a cat licking, sorry, grooming its butt. Once, memorably, Taylor Swift posted her cat doing this very thing on Insta. But what is this pose meant to be saying? “I may be a pop star or a TV celebrity, but with my flexibility and muscle tone, I am ready…
